title: On the Shafranov shift in stellarators
abstract: As first shown by Shafranov, toroidal plasmas in magnetohydrodynamic equilibrium tend to expand in major radius when the pressure is increased. Here, an average measure of the resulting Shafranov shift is introduced, and its properties are discussed for various classes of stellarator configurations. It is shown to be particularly small in quasi-helical and quasi-isodynamic stellarators with a large number of field periods, which are thus relatively robust to variations in the plasma pressure.

title: Half-Life Measurements of $^{110}$Sn, $^{113}$Sn, $^{117\mathrm{m}}$Sn, and $^{123\mathrm{m}}$Sn Produced via Photon Activation of Natural Tin
abstract: We report independent determinations of the ground-state half-lives of $^{110}$Sn, $^{113}$Sn, and the isomeric states $^{117\mathrm{m}}$Sn (J$^π = 11/2^{-}$) and $^{123\mathrm{m}}$Sn (J$^π = 3/2^{+}$), produced via photon activation of natural tin using a TT-300HE Rhodotron accelerator. The activated samples were monitored over several months using a high-purity germanium (HPGe) detector. Time-dependent $γ$-ray spectra were analyzed using Gaussian peak fitting for the \SI{280.49}{keV}, \SI{391.697}{keV}, \SI{158.56}{keV}, and \SI{160.34}{keV} transitions, yielding half-lives of \SI{4.165(25)}{h} for $^{110}$Sn, \SI{116.08(94)}{d} for $^{113}$Sn, \SI{13.95(1)}{d} for $^{117\mathrm{m}}$Sn, and \SI{39.95(12)}{min} for $^{123\mathrm{m}}$Sn. Agreement with Nuclear Data Sheets (NDS) recommended values is generally observed for $^{110}$Sn, $^{113}$Sn, and $^{123\mathrm{m}}$Sn, with deviations consistent within combined uncertainties when quantified using standardized differences (z-scores). In contrast, $^{117\mathrm{m}}$Sn exhibits a statistically significant deviation from the evaluated value of \SI{13.76(4)}{d}, with a z-score indicating a discrepancy well beyond expected statistical fluctuations. This result suggests a systematic difference warranting further investigation, with potential implications for applications relying on precise decay data, including calibration, dosimetry, and astrophysical modeling.

title: Phase Memory Controls Radiative Depolarization Near an Isolated Spin Resonance
abstract: Radiative depolarization near spin resonances in electron storage rings is conventionally described by correlated-sideband and local resonance-density theories, but a quantitative description of the crossover between them has remained lacking. Here we derive a unified finite-memory response from stochastic spin dynamics near an isolated resonance. By separating the coherent resonance contribution from stochastic fluctuations, we show that the connected correlation of the accumulated resonance-relative spin phase determines the leading off-center weak-resonance depolarization rate. Both conventional theories emerge as controlled asymptotic limits of this response, which also captures the surviving synchrotron phase memory governing the crossover. Monte Carlo spin tracking validates the predicted rates throughout the crossover and reproduces the recurrence-induced generalized-sideband structure. More broadly, the connected-correlation formulation provides a basis for extending radiative depolarization theory to more general stochastic spin-orbit dynamics in storage rings.

title: Nonlocal Evolution of Magnetic Helicity across the Magnetohydrodynamic-Kinetic Interface
abstract: Magnetic helicity is typically indistinguishable from noise in the solar wind inertial range. Using Parker Solar Probe measurements (0.1-0.8 au), we report a robust bihelical structure emerging at the magnetohydrodynamic (MHD)-kinetic interface. This structure, formed by a striking pair of positive and negative peaks, exhibits a systematic spectral migration toward lower frequencies with increasing heliocentric distance. Crucially, this evolution deviates from local kinetic scaling laws, such as the radial decline of the ion cyclotron frequency, reflecting a nonlocal evolution of magnetic topology. Our findings provide a new observational constraint on both nonlocal MHD transport processes and the nature of the helicity barrier in the kinetic regime.

title: Cryogenic characterisation of the FBK NUV-HD-cryo Silicon Photomultipliers for the DarkSide-20k dark matter experiment
abstract: Liquid Argon Time Projection Chambers (TPCs) are highly promising detectors for dark matter searches due to their uniform response, scalability to large target masses, and compatibility with ultra-low background conditions. The DarkSide-20k (DS-20k) experiment, currently under construction at Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare (INFN) Laboratori Nazionali del Gran Sasso (LNGS), aims to achieve unprecedented sensitivity to Weakly Interacting Massive Particles (WIMPs), approaching the neutrino fog. At the heart of the detector is a dual-phase TPC filled and surrounded by low-radioactivity argon from underground sources (i.e. Underground Argon (UAr)), functioning both as the WIMP target and detection medium. The experiment employs Fondazione Bruno Kessler (FBK) NUV-HD-cryo Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs) as the chosen photon sensors for its optical planes. Key SiPM properties such as dark noise rate, gain and direct crosstalk were measured using specialized test setups at 77 K. The photon detection efficiency (PDE) was measured under vacuum at 77 K over the wavelength range 350-820 nm. Secondary photon emission, which can give rise to external optical crosstalk, was measured under vacuum at 86 K over the wavelength range 550-1020 nm.

title: Controlling writhe in stellarator optimization
abstract: The writhe of a closed curve measures its coiling, and for a ribbon along it, writhe is the contribution to the linking number not due to twist. In stellarators, large writhe implies large helical excursion and has previously been either an uncontrolled outcome in optimization, or fixed beforehand by the choice of the coordinate system. We present a simple method to target the underlying writhe of the plasma boundary during optimization. Our method calculates writhe and linking number directly from the underlying elliptical boundary of the stellarator. It therefore does not require any properties of the MHD equilibrium solve, such as the true magnetic axis, making it fast to evaluate and smooth to differentiate. Examples for quasi-helically symmetric stellarators show that this target works well in practice.

title: Validation of geometric proxies using negative and positive triangularity plasmas with varying elongation on TCV and multi-machine gyrokinetic simulations
abstract: Negative Triangularity (NT) tokamak plasmas can achieve H-mode-like confinement while avoiding Edge Localized Modes, making them an attractive reactor scenario. Predicting in which configuration this benefit occurs requires understanding how magnetic geometry controls turbulent transport. Using a set of geometric proxies based on the poloidally averaged magnetic drift velocity, its poloidal variation, and Finite Larmor Radius (FLR) effects, this work validates their predictive power against gyrokinetic simulations and experiments. First, the proxies are used to predict how the relative benefit of NT over Positive Triangularity (PT) evolves with elongation $κ$, forecasting a detrimental effect of NT below $κ\sim0.75$--$0.8$. This prediction is confirmed by linear and nonlinear GENE simulations in both ITG- and TEM-dominated regimes. Additionally, a dedicated experimental elongation scan on TCV shows that NT plasmas at $κ^{\rm LCFS}=1.5$ have $β_N$ and $H_{98y2}$ roughly 1.5 times larger than PT counterparts, while no difference is observed at $κ^{\rm LCFS}=0.95$. The analysis is then extended to realistic ITG-dominated scenarios from DIII-D, AUG, and JET, including up-down asymmetric equilibria where conventional triangularity-based descriptions break down. In all three devices, simulations of NT equilibria exhibit substantially reduced nonlinear heat fluxes relative to PT (factors of 1.8, 1.6, and 2.1, respectively). A systematic swap of geometric coefficients between NT and PT equilibria shows that magnetic drifts and FLR effects are the dominant stabilizing mechanisms across all machines, with parallel dynamics playing a secondary role. These results establish the geometric proxies as reliable, computationally inexpensive predictors of NT transport benefits across diverse shapes and turbulence regimes.

title: Performance and Radiation Damage of the Heavy-Ion Silicon Beam Tracker in the BM@N Experiment
abstract: The Silicon Beam Tracker (SiBT) of the BM@N experiment at the NICA complex (JINR, Dubna) is designed to reconstruct trajectories of beam ions upstream of the target. It consists of three stations based on double-sided silicon strip detectors (DSSDs) installed directly in the relativistic heavy-ion beam. The SiBT performance and radiation damage were studied using data from the 2026 experimental run with $^{124}$Xe beams at~$1.6$,~$2.2$, and~$3.0$~AGeV. During the run, the leakage current of the DSSD of the third station of SiBT increased by $28.95~μ\mathrm{A}$, while the charge collection efficiency in the beam center decreased to approximately $68\%$ at the nominal bias voltage of 30~V. Increasing the bias voltage to 90~V restored the charge collection efficiency to approximately $95\%$. Despite the radiation-induced signal degradation, the tracking efficiency remained close to $99\%$. The accumulated radiation damage was also used to reconstruct the spatial distribution of the integrated beam fluence from strip-by-strip leakage-current measurements, yielding an average fluence of approximately $1.3\times10^{12}~\mathrm{n_{eq}/cm^2}$.

title: Effects of Coulomb Collisions on the Structures of Fast Magnetosonic Shocks
abstract: We present fully kinetic particle-in-cell simulations to demonstrate qualitative effects of binary Coulomb collisions on fast magnetosonic shocks. We find that with sufficiently high collisional frequencies, shock rippling and reformation can be inhibited, leading to stationary, laminar shock fronts. We observe that ion-ion collisions disrupt the motion of particles reflected back upstream that is the key for cyclical reformation. Meanwhile, the electron-ion collisions provide a Spitzer resistivity that can dissipate energy from the instability that causes shock rippling. This result helps us understand the role of collisions in laboratory shocks and possibly the outer heliosphere.

title: A modern particle-in-cell code for beam-beam simulations of future colliders
abstract: A key challenge in the design of next-generation colliders is predicting the effects of beam-beam interactions and using these predictions to optimize machine performance. Beam-beam interactions are characterized by strong focusing forces, radiative effects, and the generation of background particles. While analytical formulas provide insight into the dynamics of beam-beam interactions, these nonlinear, coupled effects are most accurately described with numerical methods. In this paper, we introduce the open-source particle-in-cell code WarpX as a modern tool for modeling the interaction point in future lepton colliders. WarpX provides high-performance execution on distributed GPU architectures within an open-source and actively maintained code base. We present convergence scans and benchmarks against the established beam-beam codes GUINEA-PIG (v1.2.2) and CAIN (v2.42) for luminosity spectra, photon emission, and secondary-particle production under a wide range of beam parameters corresponding to different collider concepts. Our results show that WarpX (v26.09) reproduces the benchmark beam-beam observables while enabling GPU-portable, extensible simulations. These results establish WarpX as a scalable platform for high-fidelity beam-beam modeling in future collider studies.

title: Non-contact lens metrology from optical flow and differentiable ray tracing
abstract: Accurate lens surface metrology is essential to determine the manufactured geometry of refractive optical elements and their deviation from the specified design. We demonstrate a transmission metrology method that reconstructs refractive lens surfaces from the displacement of a wavelet-noise-patterned mask. Lens-induced distortion is represented by a dense displacement field. A differentiable ray tracer fits the lens geometry using a calibrated near-telecentric camera model with an effective finite ray origin. We validate the method on commercial lenses. The recovered geometries agree with nominal specifications, and the plano-aspheric reconstruction is compared with chromatic confocal profilometry.

title: Dynamic Optimization Workflow for Gyrokinetic Stability and Transport
abstract: A dynamic optimization workflow for linear gyrokinetic stability that couples the gyrokinetic code CGYRO with the libEnsemble framework for ensemble management has been developed. The workflow is designed to efficiently explore multi-dimensional plasma parameter spaces and to address the practical challenges of simulation-driven optimization in fusion plasma physics, including expensive objective evaluations, unavailable gradient information, non-smoothness arising from transitions between dominant instability branches, and simultaneous multi-core simulations on high-performance computing resources. Rather than optimizing the growth rate at a single wavenumber, the objective maximizes the growth rate-to-wavenumber ratio over the ion-scale spectrum. A derivative-free, model-based optimization algorithm employs manifold sampling to handle the nonsmooth composite structure of the objective function. The approach is applied to the optimization of local magnetic flux-surface shaping parameters, with an equilibrium baseline drawn from DIII-D negative triangularity experimental parameters. The workflow is general and extensible and provides a foundation for future optimization studies involving nonlinear transport objectives and higher-dimensional parameter spaces.

title: Nonlinear Photoemission for Bright Beams in X-Band Photoinjectors
abstract: The ongoing development of low-cost and compact x-ray light sources is vital for increasing the number of experiments that can be performed at the atomic scale. One option for a compact and simple photoinjector is to operate in blow-out mode, in which a high-charge, short-bunch length electron beam self-expands by space-charge forces into a uniformly ellipsoidal shape. This mode necessitates a photoinjector whose initial electron pulse has a pulse duration on the order of $100$ fs. A photoinjector utilizing linear photoemission with an ultraviolet laser in this regime presents significant technical challenges, as many optical substrates degrade at these wavelengths. In this paper, we present an alternative design that uses nonlinear photoemission to produce electron beams with high charge and short bunch length in an X-band (9300 MHz) photoinjector. This photoinjector design produces an electron beam with a bunch charge of up to $200$ pC, an RMS bunch length of $291$ fs, a normalized transverse emittance of $1$ to $1.4$ mm$\cdot$mrad, and an energy spread of $10^{-4}$. This results in a beam brightness of $10^{18}$ A/m$^2$, which is bright enough for our beamline's purposes. We also present ongoing efforts are aimed at further increasing the electron beam brightness by using a spatial light modulator to shape the laser profile at the cathode.

title: FINESSE: A Versatile Beamline for Fundamental Interactions with Neutrons at the European Spallation SourcE
abstract: FINESSE (A Versatile Beamline for \textbf{F}undamental \textbf{I}nteractions with \textbf{N}eutrons at the \textbf{E}uropean \textbf{S}pallation \textbf{S}ourc\textbf{E}) is a proposed versatile beamline for fundamental interactions with neutrons at the European Spallation Source. Building on the HIBEAM design studies, FINESSE extends the original concept into a dual-guide beamline capable of operating either in a high-flux configuration or in a low-background configuration within a single ESS beam port. The high-flux branch is optimized for rare-process searches, including neutron--antineutron oscillations, neutron--sterile-neutron transitions, axion-like-particle searches, neutron charge measurements, and rare neutron decays. The low-background branch is designed for precision measurements requiring strong suppression of prompt and line-of-sight backgrounds, with a cryogenic neutron electric-dipole-moment experiment used as a benchmark case. A baseline exchangeable-guide concept has been developed in which only short guide sections inside the ESS bunker are exchanged, while the upstream extraction system and chopper positions remain fixed. A staged implementation, Short FINESSE, would use the upstream section of the high-flux beamline together with a compact magnetically controlled experimental region, enabling an early physics and R\&D programme before completion of the full facility. This paper summarizes the scientific case, beamline concept, guide simulations, chopper and timing system, magnetic-field control, detector developments, and staged implementation strategy. FINESSE would establish a long-term particle-physics infrastructure at ESS, providing a beamline for both discovery-driven searches and precision neutron measurements throughout the lifetime of the facility.

title: TD-Link: A Daisy-Chain Optical Architecture for Integrated Data Readout and Deterministic Timing Distribution in Large-Scale Detector Systems
abstract: TD-Link is an optical communication architecture that combines high-throughput data readout and sub-nanosecond timing synchronization over a single fiber for large-scale detector systems. It adopts a multidrop daisy-chain ring topology connecting a Data Concentrator to up to sixteen FERS front-end boards per link, with up to eight links per concentrator. Operating at 3.125 Gb/s, TD-Link carries data, synchronization, and control traffic in the same serial stream through a token-based streaming protocol that minimizes per-hop latency and supports on-the-fly payload fragmentation. Deterministic latency is enforced at two levels. On the concentrator, transmitter lanes are aligned by using the half-full flag of the multi-gigabit transceiver (MGT) elastic buffer as a one-bit phase detector: a firmware state machine steps the transmit phase interpolator (PI) until the buffer pointer difference crosses half-depth, locking every lane to the same phase condition. On each front-end board, where the synchronization pulse must also cross from the recovered-clock to the transmit domain, the residual three-to-five-cycle ambiguity of the synchronizer is removed by a calibration-free multiphase oversampling time-to-digital converter (TDC) with 0.8 ns bins, which time-stamps the incoming edge on the transmit time base so that a scheduler regenerates it at a fixed, programmable latency. A Digital Dual Mixer Time Difference (DDMTD) circuit measures the inter-concentrator phase. Tests with CERN PicoTDC-equipped FERS boards show a board-to-board synchronization $σ$ of 24 ps on the same ring, 27 ps across transceiver quads, and 28 ps across two cascaded concentrators, against an intrinsic front-end floor of 7 ps. Over more than one thousand cold boots without re-calibration, the boot-to-boot spread of the board-to-board skew stayed below 20 ps, consistent with the 18.6 ps phase-interpolator step.

title: HOM Mitigation
abstract: Higher Order Modes (HOMs) in accelerating structures are resonant electromagnetic fields excited and left behind by charged particle bunches. They can severely degrade the beam quality in accelerators, such as the multi-bunch energy spread and transverse emittance, and therefore one must carefully study and mitigate them. In this lecture, various methods of HOM mitigation are reviewed. On one hand, one tries to avoid their existence, for example by careful design of the accelerating structures and damping systems. On the other hand, one can reduce the effect of the excited HOM fields, for example by means of fast feedbacks or beam alignment. Additionally, a few ways to make HOM signals useful are referred to, such as diagnostics of the beam or of accelerating structures.

title: Anomaly Detection in Bunch Oscillations for Early Warning of Sudden Beam Loss at SuperKEKB
abstract: Sudden beam loss (SBL) events at the SuperKEKB collider result in the loss of a large fraction of the stored beam within just a few revolutions, on a timescale comparable to or shorter than the 20-30 μs latency of the existing abort system. Such events have damaged collimators and threaten Belle II subdetectors. Bunch Oscillation Recorders (BORs) capture transverse bunch positions at each revolution, which often show sizable oscillations that precede significant beam current loss. We test whether these precursors can be detected earlier than a charge-based reference that mimics the existing abort sensors. We apply several oscillation-based anomaly detection algorithms to 208 SBL events recorded in the low-energy ring during the 2024 run period, ranging from simple rolling statistics to machine learning models trained to forecast bunch oscillation. On 173 events not used for training or calibration, the best-balanced model (DeepLSTM) triggers before the charge-based reference in 86-90% of events across five training seeds, with a mean lead time of 25-30 μs. The only trigger classified as a false alarm fires on an oscillation that begins about 60 turns before the abort and persists until the beam is lost, making it more likely an early precursor than a spurious trigger. These results establish bunch oscillations as a viable early abort trigger and motivate a shadow-mode deployment to measure the false-alarm rate in continuous operation.

title: The fixed boundary plasma equilibrium basis for a one Gigawatt electric stellarator power plant
abstract: A fixed boundary stellarator equilibrium capable of producing 3 GW of fusion power (1 GW-electric) is presented as the design basis for the GIGA fusion power plant being developed by Gauss Fusion GmbH. The stellarator concept provides a steady-state, transient free, low recirculating power approach to a fusion power plant, which builds on 50 years of progress in plasma physics. A set of requirements for a fixed boundary equilibrium were determined through application of 0.5 D modeling. Optimization of a modified Wendelstein 7-X (W7-X) equilibrium was performed to achieve these requirements including alpha power confinement greater than $85\%$, neoclassical effective ripple below 0.01, bootstrap current below 50 kA, and reduced turbulent heat fluxes. In order to fix the plasma volume of $1500~m^3$ during optimization, the VMEC code was modified to renormalize the boundary coefficient to the desired plasma volume. The STELLOPT stellarator optimization code was modified as well to include new bootstrap current targets, a new target for the radial electric field, and the capability to hold the magnetic field on axis at a fixed value. An intermediary conceptual design plasma and final evolved fixed boundary equilibria are compared to the original modified W7-X equilibrium. The final evolved equilibrium is shown to achieve all the necessary requirements for the GIGA fusion power plant through more detailed modeling of stability, fast ion confinement, and transport.

title: Programmable Hard-X-Ray Spectral Comb Generation via Laser-Compton Scattering
abstract: Independent control of line spacing and offset underpins programmable frequency-comb spectroscopy, yet it has not been established for hard-X-ray sources based on inverse Compton scattering after electron transport and angular collection. Self-consistent multi-particle tracking and Li'enard-Wiechert radiation calculations model a transported 10 pC beam and its angle-integrated spectrum near 11 keV. Laser pulse separation programs the comb spacing, while pulse-to-pulse phase translates the entire line grid at fixed spacing. The spacing model agrees within 0.52%, while transport and optics change the phase-transfer slope by less than 0.2%. At fixed electron spot size, the largest resolvable separation scales as the inverse square of normalized emittance; subnanometer bunches also produce a mode-locked train with 13.9 as spacing. This two-coordinate programmability enables phase-stepped multicolor measurements and offers routes to hard-X-ray Ramsey interferometry, coherent control of core and nuclear excitations, and attosecond nonlinear spectroscopy.

title: A simple procedure for generating a Kappa distribution in PIC simulation
abstract: For kinetic modeling of plasma processes in space, a rejection-sampling procedure for generating a Kappa distribution in particle-in-cell (PIC) simulation is proposed. A Pareto distribution is employed as an envelope distribution. The procedure only requires uniform variates, and its acceptance efficiency is $\approx 0.73$--$0.8$.

title: Characterizing the energy resolution of the MicroBooNE LArTPC at the MeV scale using monoenergetic features of $^{208}$Tl decays
abstract: A detailed understanding of the capabilities and fidelity of low-energy reconstruction is crucial for taking advantage of MeV-scale neutrino physics opportunities in liquid argon time projection chambers (LArTPCs). This study presents a measurement of the resolution of reconstructed energy in the MicroBooNE LArTPC at $\approx 1.5$ MeV. The characterization is performed using monoenergetic signals generated by $2.614$ MeV $γ$-rays from $^{208}$Tl decays undergoing pair production in the detector. The resolution is found to be ($7.52 \pm 0.78 \text{(stat)} \pm 0.92 \text{(syst)}$)%. This value is consistent with the MicroBooNE simulation prediction of ($9.70 \pm 0.65 \text{(stat)}$)% at the $1.6 σ$ level. This study represents the first ever measurement of LArTPC energy resolution at the MeV scale and provides a pathway for monoenergetic energy calibrations in future experiments using LArTPC detectors.

title: Generalized Beth--Uhlenbeck entropy formula from the $Φ-$derivable approach
abstract: We derive a generalized Beth-Uhlenbeck formula for the entropy of a dense fermion system with strong two-particle correlations, including scattering states and bound states. We work within the $Φ-$derivable approach to the thermodynamic potential. The formula takes the form of an energy-momentum integral over a statistical distribution function times a unique spectral density. In the near mass-shell limit, the spectral density reduces, contrary to naïve expectations, not to a Lorentzian but rather to a "squared Lorentzian" shape. The relation of the Beth-Uhlenbeck formula to the $Φ$-derivable approach is exact at the two-loop level for $Φ$. The formalism we develop, which extends the Beth-Uhlenbeck approach beyond the low-density limit, includes Mott dissociation of bound states, in accordance with Levinson's theorem, and the self-consistent back reaction of correlations in the fermion propagation. We discuss applications to further systems, such as quark matter and nuclear matter.

title: QUARZ: a quasi-static particle-in-cell code with non-uniform radial grids for plasma wakefields
abstract: We present a quasi-static particle-in-cell scheme for beam-driven plasma wakefields in cylindrical geometry that works on an arbitrary non-uniform radial grid. The field equations are discretized with hat-function finite elements and conservative finite volumes on any monotone set of radial nodes, and the transverse magnetic field is obtained explicitly, without iterations, following Baxevanis and Stupakov. An optional azimuthal mode $m=1$ describes beam offsets, tilts and hosing. The discretization keeps the discrete Gauss law exact, deposits a uniform plasma exactly on every node including the axis, and remains second-order accurate on smoothly stretched grids. Resolution can therefore be placed where the physics needs it. For a tightly focused witness beam that pulls the plasma ions onto the axis, a grid that is fine only near the axis gives the same near-axis fields as a uniform grid with the same axis resolution, with thirty times fewer cells and in thirty times less computing time. Such a grid also resolves the singular closure of a cold-plasma bubble, which a uniform grid hides by smoothing it over one cell; smoothing the plasma sources over a fixed length, chosen independently of the grid, regularizes the closure and makes the wake behind it converge. The scheme is implemented in the open-source C++/Kokkos code QUARZ (Quasistatic Arbitrary-resolution RZ), which runs on CPUs and GPUs and uses MPI with a pipelined decomposition along the co-moving coordinate. Simulations of the self-modulation of the AWAKE proton bunch agree with the three-dimensional code HiPACE++. QUARZ is, to our knowledge, the first production-grade simulation code in plasma physics that is \emph{zero-touch}: all of its source code, tests and documentation were written by an AI agent directed by a physicist who did not write a single line of the code.

title: Collisionless and collisional kinetics of a plasma atmosphere with spatially and temporally intermittent heating at its base
abstract: The solar corona exhibits a pronounced temperature inversion, with plasma temperatures increasing by nearly two orders of magnitude from the chromosphere to the corona. We investigate how spatially sparse and temporally intermittent stochastic heating at the base of the transition region shapes the temperature and density structure of coronal loops within a kinetic framework. Stochastic thermal boundary conditions and surface coarse graining are introduced. Analytical solutions are derived in the collisionless limit for heating-event time scales shorter or longer than the particle crossing time, and Coulomb collisions are incorporated through a reduced kinetic model describing the thermalization of suprathermal particles. In the short-time-scale regime, spatial filling factor and temporal intermittency combine into a single effective parameter controlling the suprathermal population, producing a transition region and a hot corona both within individual loops and after coarse graining. Collisions preserve this thermal structure while reducing the coronal density through progressive thermalization. In the long-time-scale regime, individual loops are nearly isothermal and the temperature inversion emerges only after coarse graining, depending solely on the spatial filling factor. Here, Coulomb collisions and optically thin radiative losses have only minor effects, while density and temperature profiles remain broadly consistent with coronal observations. These results show that sparse, intermittent heating naturally generates suprathermal particle distributions and reproduces the observed thermal structure of the solar corona within a kinetic framework, highlighting the different sensitivity of the two regimes to collisional effects.

title: Stellarator island divertor shape optimization for reduced peak heat fluxes
abstract: An automated algorithm to construct island divertors for stellarators is presented and used to find divertors that meet heat load requirements determined by material limits. The algorithm uses just two initial conditions: two starting coordinates on the island separatrix chosen by the user. We leverage the simplicity of the algorithm to explore the divertor parameter space in a fixed magnetic equilibrium. Heat loads are approximated using the field line diffusion model implemented in the \texttt{FLARE} code. Divertor solutions that satisfy heat load requirements while maintaining a high power fraction captured are found using a parameter scan and a Bayesian optimization routine. The optimization finds divertors that perform the same as the parameter scan, but with a 75\% reduction in computational cost. The resulting divertors satisfy heat load requirements across varying cross-field heat diffusivities. Optimization over various islands in the equilibrium shows that it is easiest to find divertors that satisfy heat flux requirements for low-elongation islands. This algorithm presents a simple parameterization for island divertors and facilitates further physics and optimization studies.

title: 1/f frequency-noise reduction in nanomechanical resonators by dissipation dilution
abstract: The frequency noise of a resonant nanomechanical sensor is well understood down to its thermomechanical limit, but the longest useful averaging time is set by a flicker, or $1/f$, frequency-noise floor whose origin has remained unknown. We show that this floor is the thermal noise of the tension. By the fluctuation-dissipation theorem, the tension of a resonator with fixed ends fluctuates by an amount set by the loss angle of its material; for structural damping, these fluctuations produce $1/f$ frequency noise with a flicker coefficient $h_{-1}=E k_{\mathrm{B}} T/(2πVσ_0^2 Q_{\mathrm{el}})$, with $Q_{\mathrm{el}}$ the intrinsic loss under elongation, that contains no free parameter and is diluted by the tensile stress $σ_0$ in the same way as damping is in dissipation dilution. Silicon nitride strings and membranes from 30 to 340~nm thickness follow the predicted volume scaling, the predicted $σ_0^{-2}$ dilution across resonators and within stress-engineered strings, and the predicted thickness dependence, which places noise-active two-level systems in the volume and at the surfaces of the resonators, all at the absolute level set by the independently measured intrinsic loss. The same relation accounts for published data between 78 and 296~K; below 78~K, the loss measured at the resonance no longer represents the loss probed by the noise, marking the limit of the structural-damping assumption. Dissipation dilution therefore lowers the $1/f$ floor, and the longest useful integration time of a resonant sensor is set by its prestress, volume, temperature, and intrinsic loss angle.

title: Experimental Demonstration of Soft-Tissue Muon Scattering Tomography
abstract: Muons have fascinated physicists since their discovery in cosmic rays almost a century ago. Their large mass and relatively long lifetime allow relativistic muons to traverse large amounts of matter, a property that has been exploited to probe otherwise inaccessible structures, from volcanoes and archaeological monuments to shielded nuclear materials. Here, we experimentally demonstrate for the first time that muon scattering tomography can be extended to biological soft tissue. We image an anthropomorphic thorax phantom using a 2 GeV/c muon beam at the CERN Proton Synchrotron and reconstruct its three-dimensional scattering density from the measured deflections of individual muons. Despite the weak scattering produced by tissue-equivalent materials, the reconstructed density agrees with the expectation from simulation at the percent level. Our results extend muon imaging into a previously unexplored regime and open the possibility of using muons as a complementary probe for medical imaging.

title: Readout chain of SPD DAQ system
abstract: The Spin Physics Detector (SPD) experiment at the NICA collider of the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research (JINR) aims to study the spin structure of the nucleon and spin-related phenomena. The experimental conditions, including the high interaction rate and the large number of readout channels, require a triggerless data acquisition system with high throughput and a scalable architecture.   This work presents a hardware implementation of the readout chain that extends the previously proposed SPD DAQ architecture. The chain is based on two levels of concentrators. The L1 concentrator provides the interface between the front-end electronics and the next system level and distributes synchronous signals. The L2 concentrator aggregates data streams from several L1 concentrators before transmitting them to the computing system. A key feature of the L2 implementation is the offloading of data reception, buffering, and aggregation from the host CPU to the FPGA, motivated by the large number of small packets generated by the readout electronics.   The developed hardware platforms and their operating logic are presented, together with experimental results for the main interfaces and data-path components. The obtained results demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed hardware architecture and its application in a scalable SPD data acquisition system.

title: Relativistic Six-Fluid Rotating-Plasma Force-Balance Equilibria for p-11B Fusion Conditions in Spherical Tori
abstract: We formulate an axisymmetric spherical torus (ST) six-component magnetofluid equilibrium model for p_11B plasmas composed of thermal and suprathermal proton, boron, and electron fluids. The model is designed for p_11B parameter regimes where ion energies, strong current drive, energetic electron populations, and ion-electron temperature separation can render a single_fluid static_equilibrium description inadequate. It generalizes rotating_plasma equilibrium theory by incorporating relativistic thermal enthalpy corrections to the electron fluids via h(T/m_ec^2) and by constructing modified flux functions Y_α associated with canonical angular momentum for each component α. The equilibrium is determined by a Grad-Shafranov-like Ampere law for the poloidal magnetic flux Psi, algebraic density relations constrained by quasineutrality, and prescribed profile functions F_α(Y_α), T_α(Y_α) and K_α(Y_α). The manuscript includes the relativistic magnetofluid equations, the axisymmetric equilibrium formulation, the six_fluid computational method, and four numerical equilibria: two reactor_relevant ST p_11B parameter sets and two EHL-2 ST cases. The examples span toroidal beta b_T = 0.058_0.253, plasma currents I_p = 2.697_12.59 MA, and suprathermal electron temperatures T_eh = 287 keV_2.37 MeV, with h up to 19.1. Over these parameter ranges, Ampere's law accuracy, electrostatic potential accuracy, and component_resolved radial force balance can have errors ranging from 3% to below 0.1%. These results indicate that high-temperature p_11B ST equilibria can differ qualitatively from the single_fluid tokamak equilibria and require analysis of equilibrium component_resolved force balance, relativistic electron enthalpy, and explicit reproducibility diagnostics.

title: Universal Boolean Computation in Negatively Coupled Circle Map Lattices
abstract: We investigate the computational capabilities of a one-dimensional lattice of negatively   coupled circle maps in its traveling wave regime. We interpret propagating waves as information carriers and exploit their interactions to implement Boolean logic. The logical states are encoded by the propagation direction of the traveling waves, while the presence or absence of a wave at a designated output location represents the logical output. Using controlled wave collisions, we demonstrate the realization of NAND and NOR gates along with other basic gates. Since NAND and NOR operations are functionally complete, the results establish that the traveling wave regime of the negatively coupled circle-map lattice supports universal Boolean computation in principle. The demonstrated logical operations remain valid over a finite range of the coupling strength εand map parameter ω, indicating robustness of the computational scheme to parameter variations. Our results therefore demonstrate that computational functionality can emerge from the collective nonlinear dynamics of a coupled map lattice, providing a con- nection between the dynamical properties of traveling wave states and collision based information processing.

title: A Low-Temperature Tool for Acousto-electric Detection
abstract: We have developed an apparatus for the measurement of the acousto-electric effect (AEE) from room temperature to liquid nitrogen temperatures. The AEE is excited by bulk acoustic waves (BAWs) for which a lithium niobate piezoelectric actuator is employed. A very low background noise level is realized through careful electrical and mechanical design of the setup. The validity of the setup is tested by measuring the AEE in heavily doped P-type and N-type silicon. The opposite sign of the AEE signal was seen for both samples, showing dependence of the signal on the type of charge carrier being dragged by acoustic waves. The signal showed quadratic dependence on the driving voltage, which is consistent with the AEE literature. Further, a temperature dependence of the AEE signal was measured, which exhibits a monotonic increase with a rise in temperature. The ability to probe the AEE in bulk samples at low temperatures makes this setup a promising tool to investigate the AEE and related phenomena in different materials at cryogenic temperatures.

title: Implicit PIC Simulations of Hydrogen Plasmas with Intense Negative Ion Production
abstract: High-density plasma discharges in hydrogen operating at low pressures are of considerable interest for negative ion production used in many applications. Their weak collisionality requires a kinetic, nonlocal description, and a popular approach is to model such discharges numerically using the particle-in-cell (PIC) method combined with Monte Carlo collisions (MCC). However, the most commonly used explicit momentumconserving variant of this method is highly inefficient because it must resolve both the Debye length and the plasma period. In this context, the implicit energy-conserving PIC/MCC scheme appears to be an attractive alternative, as it can model the plasmas of interest using their actual parameters without resorting to artificial scaling techniques. This work considers simulations of two types of high-density plasma discharges performed using electromagnetic or electrostatic energy-conserving PIC/MCC codes in hydrogen, and discusses the observed negative ion production.

title: Existence and Smoothing for a Nondivergence-Form Degenerate Diffusion from Plasma-Wave Theory
abstract: We prove existence, positive-time smoothing, and physical admissibility of weak solutions to the degenerate parabolic Cauchy-Dirichlet problem $\partial_t u = ρ_λ(x) u \partial_x^2 u + ρ_λ(x) g(x) u$ on the half-line, where $ρ_λ$ vanishes at the boundary and grows at infinity. This scalar problem arises by formally reducing the system of equations given by the quasilinear theory of plasma waves in the one-dimensional case. This theory models a background distribution of electrons $f$ coupled to a spectral energy density $W$ through wave-particle resonance. For the scalar problem we construct weak solutions from weighted $L^p$ initial data and bounded reaction, admitting the unbounded, discontinuous data that the physical model demands, and lying beyond the reach of the continuous-data theories developed for nearby problems. We identify a parabolic smoothing effect for the constructed solution, namely one-sided bounds on $\partial_t u$: from merely integrable data, the solution becomes locally Hölder in space and time and locally Lipschitz in space at positive times. This spatial regularity is shown to be sharp by explicit examples. Finally, we address the quasilinear system itself, whose well-posedness remains open: we prove that the scalar solution induces a particle-wave pair $(f^{\ast}, W^{\ast})$ which is a weak solution of the system. Under nonnegativity and finite-moment hypotheses on the initial data, both components remain nonnegative and the initial mass is conserved. Moreover, the pair inherits positive-time regularity, with $W^{\ast}$ decaying quantitatively at large wavenumber and $f^{\ast}$ smoothing to a locally bounded function even when initially a measure.

title: Radial increase of the compensated interplanetary magnetic field magnitude as a result of the growth of spherically polarized Alfvén waves
abstract: Measurements from the NASA Parker Solar Probe (PSP) mission demonstrate that inside $\sim20$ solar radii ($\Rs$) the magnitude of the interplanetary magnetic field does not fall off simply as $1/R^2$, with $\avg{|B|}\,R^2$ 15--20\% below its value at $\sim60\,\Rs$. Here we use PSP magnetic field measurements over $10.6$--$56.8\,\Rs$ to show that the outward rise of $\avg{|B|}\,R^2$ is not due to the global structure of the heliospheric magnetic field or proximity to the heliospheric current sheet but is the direct result of the growth of large-amplitude, spherically polarized Alfvén waves (so-called `switchbacks'). Over the same distance range, $\avg{B_R}\,R^2$ stays constant, so that the sector-signed radial flux is conserved. The wave amplitude $ε= B_{\perp,{\rm rms}}/\avg{B_\parallel}$ grows from $0.26$ to $0.57$ as $R^{1/2}\cosα$, and $\avg{|B|}/\avg{B_R}$ rises by $20\%$. A simple model parametrized by the broadening of the distribution of deflection angles reproduces the effect to high accuracy. These results demonstrate that as the relative wave amplitudes grow with increasing solar distance, a dynamo-like process operates to enhance the field magnitude by up to $20\%$. By enhancing magnetic pressure this has implications for the large scale solar wind structure in the low-beta inner heliosphere, as well as partially resolving the long-standing discrepancy between remote measurements of the solar magnetic field and those made in situ by earlier missions farther from the Sun.

title: Broadband 600- and 1200-GHz Subharmonically Pumped Schottky Diode Mixers
abstract: A subharmonic mixer topology is introduced that uses quarter-wave stubs to create virtual RF/LO grounds and provide impedance matching in close proximity to the antiparallel Schottky barrier diode pair, thereby reducing the electrical length and enabling broadband operation. The RF/LO matching topology is demonstrated at 600 GHz and 1200 GHz, with good agreement between measured and simulated performance. The 600-GHz mixer demonstrates approximately 20% RF bandwidth with a DSB receiver noise temperature below 1300 K across most of the measured band, while the 1200-GHz implementation achieves DSB receiver noise temperatures below 3000 K over a broad frequency range. Both mixers are characterized at room temperature with approximately 2 mW of LO power. The 600-GHz mixer is used in the Submillimeter Wave Instrument (SWI) onboard ESA's Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer. Overall, these results demonstrate state-of-the-art room-temperature performance for broadband receiver front ends targeting atmospheric research and remote-sensing applications.

title: Brilliance: toward autonomous computational research in particle accelerator physics
abstract: Computational research in physics requires continuous interplay between simulation and scientific interpretation, demanding substantial specialist effort. Here we introduce Brilliance, a research agent that combines large language models, reusable physics knowledge and numerical simulation to conduct adaptive investigations in accelerator physics. Given a single user prompt, Brilliance designs a fourth-generation synchrotron light source that meets coupled emittance and nonlinear-acceptance requirements. Further exploration yields a design combining sub-10-pm emittance with a large dynamic aperture under realistic engineering constraints, suggesting a route towards hard-X-ray diffraction-limited operation, although the momentum-acceptance target remains unmet. Brilliance also calibrates a model of an operating light source against measured responses, accurately inferring its lattice and calibration errors. Across these studies, Brilliance autonomously revises its computational strategies in response to numerical evidence. These results demonstrate a route towards delegating sustained scientific investigations to agents equipped with domain expertise and numerical tools.

title: Polarized quantum effects in countable signals from intense laser - electron beam interactions
abstract: We investigate the feasibility of precision counting experiments based on laser-electron beam interactions to verify strong-field quantum electrodynamic effects, with particular emphasis on the stochastic nature of photon emission, photon polarization, and spin asymmetry. A precise Monte-Carlo model is developed using photon packets with multi-dimensional phase-space weighting, hierarchical-mesh cumulative distribution functions, and a variable time-step method. This model quantitatively reproduces the highest edge of the photon energy spectrum and the positron yield in the previous SLAC E-144 experiment. The quantized radiation back-reaction determines the highest edge tail and thus the positron yield for higher laser intensities. The spin asymmetry in photon emission and spin flip determines photon polarization in the high-energy tail, while that in pair production can be observed through the large-angle positron scattering. Our simulations predict that these effects depend on the combination of the electron-beam energy and the laser intensity, and that they could be verified in future ELI-NP experiments using sub-GeV electron beams and optical lasers with intensities ~10^22W/cm2.

title: A reduced model for neoclassical transport in non-axisymmetric magnetic configurations
abstract: A unified framework is proposed to compute a neoclassical equilibrium for tokamaks with non-axisymmetric magnetic perturbations, based on a Hamiltonian description combined with a variational approach that relies on a principle of minimum entropy production. This approach allows for a transparent identification of the respective contributions from different classes of trapped particles in magnetic well minima. Analytic expressions are derived for specific collisionality regimes, and a fast and efficient numerical procedure is devised to compute the entropy production rate. Finding the extremum of the entropy production leads to tractable expressions of transport coefficients that can be computed quickly and efficiently.

title: Femtosecond Three-Dimensional Imaging of Single-Protein with Hard X-ray Laser
abstract: The extremely intense pulses of X-ray free-electron lasers (XFELs) have enabled imaging of radiation-sensitive samples, such as macromolecular microcrystals, beyond radiation damage limits. These sources have the potential to deliver biomolecular single-particle imaging, similar to cryo-electron microscopy but without the need for cryo-fixation and with temporal resolution from femtoseconds to milliseconds. While this possibility was recognized before XFELs were built, the biological single-particle imaging work-flow has previously only been demonstrated on large virus particles. Based on decades of improvements in X-ray beam focusing, particle delivery, diffraction detection, and advanced analysis, here we demonstrate imaging of a single molecular complex, the giant-hemoglobin erythrocruorin (Ery) with X-ray laser pulses. Two-dimensional classes of diffraction patterns could be reconstructed to 15 Angstrom resolution, and 3D images to approximately 20 Angstrom, while the 3D merged intensity in reciprocal space extended beyond 20 Angstrom. The resolution discrepancy is likely due to heterogeneity caused by gas-phase compaction of the complexes. With increased throughput, this approach could be used to reveal in-situ structural details during mass spectrometry studies of biomolecules, while improvements in sample delivery may provide ultrafast snapshot imaging of biological single-particles in their native-state beyond the limitations of radiation damage.

title: Nonreciprocal Polychromatic Radiation from a Space-Time-Modulated Omega-Topology Meta-Transceiver
abstract: Time-modulated metasurfaces offer a magnet-free route to nonreciprocal wave control, but existing realizations modulate only the electric response of the structure, and proposals for simultaneous electric-magnetic modulation have so far remained theoretical. We experimentally demonstrate a space-time-periodic meta-transceiver whose omega-topology unit cell integrates varactor-loaded electric (dipole) and magnetic (ring) resonators, both modulated by a common unidirectional traveling-wave bias. This modulation gives rise to two independent, experimentally resolved manifestations of nonreciprocity: on transmit, the incident field is efficiently converted into a polychromatic comb of harmonics that radiate at distinct, bias-reconfigurable angles, while on receive, the same modulation instead suppresses frequency conversion and routes the incoming wave preferentially toward one port over the other. These two effects - nonreciprocal polychromatic conversion and unidirectional wave routing - arise from a single unidirectional space-time modulation but act on distinct physical observables, frequency content and spatial direction, respectively. Measured near the electric resonance with a shared bias, these effects characterize the complete cell and do not separate its electric and magnetic contributions. Our results establish the space-time-modulated omega-topology cell as an experimentally viable platform for reconfigurable, full-duplex nonreciprocal wave transformation.

title: Dual deconvolution multifocal fluorescence response matrix microscopy for aberration-free high-throughput super-resolution imaging
abstract: Fluorescence response matrix imaging enables separate computational correction of excitation and emission aberrations through dual deconvolution, but single-focus acquisition requires a large number of camera frames, limiting its practical use. Multifocal excitation can accelerate acquisition by recording many illumination positions in parallel, but denser foci also increase inter-focus crosstalk, which can bias the estimated excitation and emission optical transfer functions and degrade aberration correction. Here, we introduce high-throughput aberration-free fluorescence response matrix imaging with adaptive multifocal illumination, in which the inter-focus spacing of the multifocal lattice is adjusted according to specimen-dependent crosstalk. A programmable digital micromirror device generates multifocal excitation lattices, and the resulting detector-resolved fluorescence responses are assembled into a two-coordinate fluorescence response matrix. Dual deconvolution separately estimates and corrects the excitation and emission optical transfer functions, and the aberration-corrected matrix is then combined in the spatial-frequency domain to reconstruct the aberration-free image. This strategy reduces the number of required camera frames by approximately three orders of magnitude, allowing response matrices with $\sim 10^6$ illumination positions to be acquired within seconds to a few minutes. The accelerated acquisition preserves the aberration-correction capability of dual deconvolution and achieves an estimated lateral resolution of $\sim$100 nm. Applied to heterogeneous mouse brain and kidney tissue, the method enables high-resolution, depth-resolved volumetric imaging while correcting specimen-dependent aberrations. Together, these results establish adaptive multifocal illumination as a practical route to high-throughput aberration-free fluorescence response matrix imaging.

title: High-throughput full-f gyrokinetics of the tokamak boundary
abstract: Full-f gyrokinetics of the tokamak boundary have so far been limited to individual, expert-curated cases. We report hundreds of concurrent and unsupervised simulations of the edge and scrape-off layer (SOL) in a geometry based on the Tokamak à Configuration Variable (TCV), scanning triangularity, elongation and heating power, each evolving turbulence for more than a millisecond, i.e. about two energy confinement times. Without tuned transport coefficients or experimental inputs, the ensemble reproduces the range of SOL heat-flux decay lengths measured in TCV, as well as the reduced SOL density fluctuations and the improved confinement of negative triangularity. The effect of triangularity on confinement is power dependent. At high power, negative triangularity improves the ion energy confinement by weakening the dominant microinstability rather than by a stronger sheared flow. At low power, positive triangularity flattens the ion temperature profile across the separatrix, which we attribute to a longer distance between the trapped ions and the cold recycling source. Local linear gyrokinetic calculations and the transport coefficients extracted from the turbulent fluxes consistently indicate a trapped-electron-mode regime, in which the conductive heat flux at the separatrix is carried by the electrons and the ion energy transport is convective. This article details the simulation setup, the ensemble statistics and the verification of the results, which are also summarized in a companion Letter.

title: Plasma-neutral collision operators for hydrogen isotopes: kinetic and gyrokinetic descriptions, comparison to fluid
abstract: Plasma-neutral interactions critically affect the edge dynamics of magnetically confined fusion devices. Neutral atoms modify ion and electron velocity distributions, potentially affecting local instabilities Standard fluid models simplify these processes (namely charge exchange, ionization and recombination) using Maxwellian assumptions and linearized source terms. We revisit these assumptions for a hydrogen plasma interacting with hydrogen atoms. We derive plasma-neutral interaction terms in the kinetic and gyrokinetic frameworks. Accounting for velocity-dependent differential cross-sections, the model captures the kinetic impact of inelastic collisions on ions and electrons beyond energy and momentum exchange. We demonstrate that the fluid moments of the kinetic model reduce to standard fluid source terms under the appropriate assumptions of Maxwellianity and linearity. We compare the kinetic model with fluid models through their effects on distribution functions and fluid moments. Substantial discrepancies are observed, even for Maxwellian distributions. For charge exchange, the kinetic model yields momentum and energy exchange rates up to twice those predicted by fluid descriptions. We show that a fluid treatment of ionization greatly overestimates the mean kinetic energy of the produced electrons. These results highlight the limitations of fluid descriptions and the importance of kinetic effects in edge-plasma momentum and energy exchange.

title: Toward a Multimodal Foundation Model for Plasma State Reconstruction
abstract: Plasma experiments observe coupled physical states through sparse, heterogeneous, and incomplete diagnostics. We present a proof of concept toward a multimodal foundation model for plasma state reconstruction during magnetic reconnection, motivated by the Facility for Laboratory Reconnection Experiments (FLARE). Using 250 synthetic VPIC simulations at fixed reference electron beta $β_{e0}=0.2$, with 225 training runs and 25 disjoint validation runs, we train a 5.5M-parameter residual 3D U-Net to reconstruct three magnetic-field components and electron density from incomplete observations. The model combines spatial-only pooling, which preserves all 24 temporal frames, with global spatiotemporal self-attention and rotary positional encoding. Independently masking magnetic and density modalities across random, grid, block, and temporal patterns enables sparse sensing, cross-modal completion, density super-resolution, and temporal completion with a single set of weights and no task-specific retraining. With density fully hidden, just 0.1% magnetic spatial visibility reduces median density NRMSE from approximately 0.9 to 0.1. Conversely, observed density improves current-density reconstruction when magnetic data are absent or extremely sparse. With no magnetic observations, roughly 1% density visibility approaches the density reconstruction accuracy achieved with fully observed magnetic fields, although current structure remains more dependent on direct magnetic measurements. Full magnetic conditioning also stabilizes completion of missing future density frames. These results demonstrate bidirectional cross-modal predictive coupling within this simulation regime. Generalization across plasma regimes or to experimental measurements remains untested.

title: Prediction of the thermal neutron response of grain-boundary impedance in Gd-doped ceria based on the radiation-ionic effect
abstract: The radiation-ionic effect was recently reported in 3 mol% Gd-doped CeO$_2$ (3GDC): under $^{60}$Co gamma irradiation at 35 Gy/min, the grain-boundary (GB) ionic resistance of a bulk pellet decreased 680-fold at room temperature, because electrons trapped at the GB core lower the space-charge potential. The effect has been demonstrated only with photons. Gd has the largest thermal-neutron capture cross section of any stable element and is also the dopant that creates the GB barrier in GDC, so the same mechanism could link GB impedance to thermal-neutron sensing; whether it does, and under what conditions, has not been examined. Here the thermal-neutron response of 3GDC is modelled with the gamma-calibrated Mott-Schottky/Seager framework, with unmeasured parameters carried as intervals and propagated jointly. Each capture deposits about 50 keV by conversion and Auger electrons within 1 $μ$m, the remaining 8 MeV leaving as prompt photons; Gd segregation to the GBs adds a factor of only 1-2 because the electron range exceeds the grain size. A thermal flux of $8\times10^{9}$ cm$^{-2}$s$^{-1}$ (6-12$\times10^{9}$) matches the GB-effective generation rate of the 35 Gy/min calibration, and the predicted room-temperature GB resistance ratio is 110 (70-170) at $10^{9}$ and 970 (600-1500) at $10^{10}$ cm$^{-2}$s$^{-1}$, falling to 2 at 61 (55-68) and 81 (73-92) $^\circ$C. The neutron case differs from gamma irradiation in three respects: capture events are discrete, so the continuous-source approximation depends on the unmeasured trapped-charge lifetime; self-shielding (mean free path 0.27 mm) makes the response thickness dependent; and capture photons absorbed in the pellet add a gamma term comparable to the local term for pellets of 0.3 mm or more. The intervals are conditional on the model and exclude its structural error. The conditions under which the prediction can be tested are given.

title: Development of high-resolution timing technique in the past 25 years
abstract: This paper reviews recent progress in high-resolution timing, rate capability, and aging performance of particle detectors in the context of developments over the past 25 years. It focuses on MCP, SiPM, LGAD, 3D silicon, and SiEM detectors and compares their performance with that of gaseous timing detectors. In addition, preliminary results from a simplified simulation program, Mini-TCAD, are presented, indicating that hexagonal 3D silicon cells may provide better drift-time uniformity and timing resolution than square cells.

title: Multi-Objective Design of C-Shaped Targets for Energy--Divergence Control in Laser-Driven Proton Acceleration
abstract: We optimize the energy-divergence trade-off of laser-driven protons from a C-shaped target using two-dimensional particle-in-cell simulations and constrained multi-objective Bayesian optimization. Five geometry and focusing parameters are varied to maximize proton cutoff energy and minimize the RMS divergence of forward protons with E_k >= 5 MeV under a proton-only conversion-efficiency constraint of eta_H >= 9%. Of 82 designs, 60 are feasible and 15 Pareto-optimal. The Max-Energy and Min-Divergence endpoints yield 28.64 MeV at 52.51 degrees and 11.47 MeV at 11.13 degrees, respectively; a representative compromise yields 21.44 MeV at 38.44 degrees. Matched-stage diagnostics link these regimes to optical-field buildup, electron energization, charge separation, and outer-sheath organization. Numerical tests support the principal trends. Reflection timing does not support a monotonic trapping-duration law, and the charge-sheath relation remains non-local. These results establish a design-resolved route to controlling proton energy and angular quality.

title: In-situ Generation of Polarized Attosecond Positron Bunches via Radiation-Wakefield Induced Two-Photon Pairs
abstract: High-energy, dense, spin-polarized positron beams with attosecond duration are highly desirable for advanced accelerator physics, laboratory astrophysics, and ultrafast matter-antimatter studies, yet remain beyond the capability of conventional source and injection-based plasma-acceleration schemes. We propose an integrated in-situ method for production, trapping, and accelerating polarized attosecond positron bunches in a single plasma stage. An ultraintense hollow laser propagating in a plasma channel drives a radiative wakefield, where longitudinally injected electrons emit a dense MeV gamma-ray bath through nonlinear Compton scattering. Subsequent photon-photon collisions induce linear Breit-Wheeler pair production, while linear and nonlinear radiative processes mediate polarization transfer to the produced positrons. Spin-resolved QED particle-in-cell simulations indicate that the laser-modulated wakefield naturally captures positrons born in the frontier bubble wake, forming collimated bunch trains with hundred-attosecond duration, GeV-level energies, and densities up to 10^17 cm^-3. Parameter scans demonstrate robustness against variations of laser intensity and plasma-channel density. This single-shot, source-free approach simultaneously addresses positron production, polarization, temporal compression, and plasma injection, offering a compact route toward polarized attosecond antimatter beams.

title: First achievement of 100 million degree electron temperatures in a spherical torus: the EXL-50U
abstract: Here,we report an ST plasma in which Thomson scattering measures a central electron temperature exceeding 8.6 keV (100 million degrees kelvin) on the EXL-50U spherical torus device.The high-temperature phase is obtained at low density by sequential operation of two 50 GHz ECRH systems: ordinary-mode (O-mode) ECRH3 followed by extraordinary-mode (X-mode) ECRH4. In contrast to neutral-beam-heated high-ion-temperature ST scenarios, the discharge is sustained by ECRH only.

title: SPIRE: Spin-Resolved Particle-in-Cell with Radiative Corrections for Extreme Laser--Plasma Interactions
abstract: We present SPIRE, a spin- and photon-polarization-resolved particle-in-cell (PIC) code for self-consistent simulations of laser-plasma interactions in the strong-field quantum electrodynamics (QED) regime. The classical PIC framework combines a Yee-grid finite-difference time-domain Maxwell solver, a relativistic Boris particle pusher, shape-function particle-grid interpolation, Esirkepov charge-conserving current deposition, laser boundary injection, and a relativistic moving window in one, two, and three spatial dimensions. A vectorial Laguerre-Gaussian laser injector based on an angular-spectrum formulation supports tightly focused, nonparaxial optical orbital-angular-momentum modes. The strong-field QED module treats nonlinear Compton scattering and nonlinear Breit-Wheeler pair production as stochastic processes using spin- and polarization-resolved probabilities in the local constant-field approximation. Electron and positron spin evolution includes stochastic transitions, no-emission corrections, and Thomas-Bargmann-Michel-Telegdi precession with a field-dependent anomalous magnetic moment. Photon polarization is represented by the Stokes vector and evolves through nonlinear Compton scattering, pair production, vacuum birefringence, and vacuum dichroism. The implementation is verified with one-, two-, and three-dimensional benchmarks. Classical PIC results are cross-checked against SMILEI, and the spin- and polarization-resolved QED modules reproduce published results for polarized electron generation, vacuum birefringence and dichroism, and dense polarized positron production. These benchmarks verify the coupled classical PIC, strong-field QED, spin, and photon-polarization modules implemented in SPIRE.
